Emergency Roof Repair and Tarping in Houston

Water running through the ceiling, a tree through the roof, a hole open to more rain. Call one free number at any hour and you are put through to an independent, locally owned roofing company in greater Houston that handles emergency calls.

Call (832) 662-4107 Is it an emergency?
  1. Home
  2. Services
  3. Emergency Roof Repair

When a roof problem is an emergency

A Houston emergency roof repair is about one thing: stopping water and weather from getting into the house tonight. The permanent fix usually comes later, once the roof is dry and the damage has been documented.

Emergency work costs more than a scheduled visit, so it helps to know which situations need it. These usually do:

  • Water running into the house, not dripping, and more rain on the way.
  • A tree or a large limb on or through the roof.
  • Daylight visible in the attic, or a section of deck torn open.
  • A ceiling that is bulging, sagging or cracking under trapped water.
  • Water near light fixtures, outlets or the attic wiring.
  • Any sag or bend in the roofline itself.

A slow drip into a bucket with a clear forecast is still worth a call, but it can usually wait for a regular appointment. The test is whether more water will come in before a roofer could get there in daylight.

Safe steps while you wait

The single most important rule: do not go up there. Roofs are slick in rain and at night, storm-damaged decking can give way, and a fall is far worse than a wet ceiling. Everything useful can be done from inside the house and from the ground.

Stay off the roof. Wet, storm-damaged roofs are slick and the decking may be weak, so leave the ladder in the garage. Keep well away from downed power lines and report them to CenterPoint Energy or 911. Indoors, move belongings away from the leak, put a bucket or towels under the drip and keep people out of any room where the ceiling sags. Photograph the damage from the ground and inside the house, then call your insurer and a roofer.

Inside the house

  • Move furniture, electronics, rugs and papers away from the water.
  • Put buckets, pans or towels under every drip and empty them before they overflow.
  • Keep children and pets out of any room with a bulging or sagging ceiling, and close the door.
  • If water is near a light fixture or outlet, stay out of that room, keep switches untouched and tell the roofer and your utility on the phone.
  • Lay plastic sheeting over anything too heavy to move.

Outside and on the phone

  • Stay well clear of downed lines, and of any limb or fence touching them. Report them to CenterPoint Energy or 911.
  • Photograph the roof and the yard from the ground, and every wet spot inside, before anything is moved or covered.
  • Call a roofer to cover the opening, and let your insurance company know about the damage.
  • Write down the time the damage happened and the time you called each one.
  • Keep every receipt, from the tarp to a hotel night.

A ceiling holding water is dangerous to stand under. Leave it to the roofer or a water damage company to deal with, and keep people out of the room until then.

What a proper emergency tarp looks like

Tarping is the roofer's job, done from the roof with the right equipment. Knowing what a good one looks like helps you judge the work and explain it to your adjuster.

Signs of a sound tarp

  • It covers the whole damaged area with room to spare on every side.
  • It runs up and over the ridge where it can, so water flows across the top of it instead of under its upper edge.
  • It is held down with wood strips fastened along its edges, so wind cannot get a grip.
  • It lies tight and flat, without loose folds that catch wind or hold water.
  • The roofer photographs the damage before covering it and the tarp once it is on.

Signs of a weak one

  • A tarp laid loosely over the hole and weighted with bricks or tires.
  • The upper edge stops below the damage, so water runs straight beneath it.
  • Flapping corners, or a tarp too small for the opening.
  • No photos of what was underneath before it was covered.
  • No date given for the permanent repair.

A tarp is a temporary bridge, not a repair. Sun and wind wear it down, so ask the roofer, before it leaves, when it will come back to inspect properly and how long it expects this cover to hold.

After some federally declared disasters, FEMA has the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers run Operation Blue Roof, which puts a temporary cover of blue plastic sheeting, fastened with wood strips, on eligible damaged roofs of primary homes at no cost once the owner signs a right of entry form. It is offered storm by storm, flat roofs and some roof types do not qualify, and the Corps warns that anyone asking you for money for a blue roof is not part of the program.

What drives the cost of an emergency call

The line does not quote prices, and no roofer can price an emergency honestly before seeing it. What moves the number is easy to understand, though, and worth asking about up front:

FactorWhy it matters
Time and weatherNight, weekend and storm-hour work is harder and slower, and many companies charge more for it.
DemandAfter a regional storm, every roofer is booked at once.
Size of the openingA large hole takes more tarp, more lumber and more time to secure.
Pitch and heightSteep and two-story roofs need more safety equipment and more care.
A tree on the roofRemoving a heavy limb may need a tree crew before any roofing can happen.
Interior damageWet insulation and drywall are a separate job, usually for a water damage company.

Ask for the emergency charge in writing before work starts, what it includes, and whether any of it is credited toward the permanent repair.

Hiring in a hurry, without getting burned

Emergencies are when people sign things they would normally read twice. The Texas Department of Insurance warns that contractors who show up uninvited after a disaster sometimes present a contract as an estimate, and that a contract should never be signed with blank spaces. Pay for the emergency cover by check or card, not cash, and do not pay in full for the permanent repair up front. Under Texas Business and Commerce Code Chapter 58, a contractor repairing natural disaster damage may not require full or partial payment before work begins, and partial payments must be proportionate to the work done and materials delivered.

Separate the two jobs on paper. The emergency cover can be agreed on the spot. The permanent repair, which may be paid from an insurance claim, deserves a written, itemized estimate, a look at the roofer's certificate of liability insurance and time for your adjuster to see the roof.

The deductible is yours to pay. The Texas Department of Insurance says it is illegal for a contractor to offer to waive, rebate or absorb your deductible, and a contract of $1,000 or more paid with insurance money must include a notice saying so. A roofer also may not act as your public adjuster on a property it works on. Treat any offer to "cover the deductible" as a reason to call someone else.

Water coming in, or a limb on the roof? Call the number and describe what you can see from the ground. The local roofing company you are put through to decides how to cover the roof and names its charge before it starts.

Questions to ask on an emergency call

Before anyone drives out

  • What is your emergency or after-hours charge, and what does it cover?
  • Will the cover be a tarp fastened with wood strips and run over the ridge?
  • Do you take care of a limb on the roof, or do I need a tree crew too?
  • What is your business address in greater Houston?

Before the crew leaves

  • Can you send me the photos from before and after the tarp went on?
  • What did you see that I should tell my insurer?
  • When will you come back to inspect and quote the permanent repair?
  • Is the emergency charge credited against that repair?

How an emergency call works on this line

Day or night, an automated assistant takes the call. Say it is an emergency, describe what you see and give your part of greater Houston, and the call is transferred to an independent roofing company. The line cannot promise how soon anyone arrives; the roofing company tells you that itself.

  1. Call the numberAn automated assistant answers (832) 662-4107 at any hour and asks which service you need, since the line also takes heating, cooling, pressure washing and water damage calls.
  2. Describe the roofA leak, missing shingles, hail, a limb on the roof or an old roof you want looked at, plus your part of greater Houston and how urgent it is.
  3. Get put throughYour call is transferred to an independent, locally owned roofing company, which hears a short summary before it picks up.
  4. Deal with the roofer directlyIt inspects, quotes and does the work, and you pay it (or your insurer does, as you arrange). If it misses the call, it gets your name, number, city and need to call you back.

Texas has no state roofing license. No state agency licenses roofing contractors in Texas, and a 2025 bill to create one (HB 3344) did not reach a vote of the full House before the session ended. So check what you can: a certificate of liability insurance sent to you, a written contract with the full scope, a permit where your city requires one, local addresses you can drive past, and the shingle maker's warranty registration. Some cities also ask roofers to register. The line does not check any of this for you. How to check a roofer before you hire.

Questions Houston homeowners ask

Is a leaking roof an emergency?

It is when water is coming in faster than a bucket can handle, when it is running near light fixtures or outlets, when a ceiling is sagging, or when the roof is open and more rain is forecast. A slow drip into a pan with dry weather ahead is urgent but can usually wait for a daytime visit. Either way, call and describe it, and the roofer can tell you how soon it needs a cover. See roof leak repair for the non-emergency kind.

Who do I call for an emergency roof leak in Houston?

For a live wire, a gas smell or anyone hurt, call 911 first, and report downed lines to CenterPoint Energy. For the roof itself, call a roofing company that takes emergency calls; this free line answers any hour and transfers you to an independent, locally owned one in greater Houston. Next, phone your insurance company and open a claim if you plan to file. Keep the storm claim checklist handy for the paperwork.

How much does emergency roof repair cost?

The line does not quote prices, and honest roofers price the job after seeing it. What drives the cost: the hour and the weather, how big the opening is, how steep and high the roof is, whether a tree has to come off first, how much tarp and lumber the cover takes, and how busy every crew is after a major storm. Ask for the emergency charge in writing before work starts, and whether it is credited against the permanent repair.

Will my insurance pay for an emergency tarp?

Ask your insurer before assuming. Ask whether your policy expects you to take reasonable steps to prevent further damage after a storm, which is what an emergency cover does, and what it reimburses for that work. The answer depends on your policy and the cause of the damage. Keep every receipt, photograph the damage before the tarp goes on, and send the roofer's invoice with your claim. The roof insurance claims guide explains deductibles.

Who actually comes out if I call this number at night?

A roofing company near you, independent and locally owned, that accepts emergency work. Houston Expert Roofers is simply the number: a recorded assistant picks up day or night, asks what is happening and where, and hands the call over. When that roofer misses the call, your name, phone, town and urgency are sent on so it can ring you back. The roofing company does the work and bills you.

Water coming in right now? Call the line

Tell the automated assistant what the roof is doing and where you live. Your call is put through to an independent, locally owned roofing company in greater Houston, which looks at the roof and gives you its own price.
